title: Emerging Legal Frameworks
answer: Machine authorship, autonomous entities, multi-agent liability, deepfake evidence and the right to an explanation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
children.blurb: The threshold of machine authorship concerns the point at which output from an AI system is treated as an authored work for legal purposes, rather than as an unowned artifact or a derivative of training data.

children.name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
children.blurb: Autonomous entities are software systems that can act with limited human oversight, enter contracts, manage assets, or make decisions.

children.name: Liability When Agents Interact
children.blurb: This page covers legal responsibility when two or more AI agents interact without a human directly approving each step.

children.name: Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards
children.blurb: Deepfakes are synthetic audio, image, or video created or altered by machine learning to depict a person saying or doing something they did not.

children.name: The Right to an Explanation
children.blurb: The right to an explanation concerns whether a person affected by an automated decision can obtain a meaningful account of how that decision was reached.

sections.body: This field is about how law responds to AI systems that create, act, and generate evidence. Machine authorship asks whether output from a model can be protected by copyright or patent, and who if anyone is the author. Autonomous entities and fiduciaries concern whether an AI can hold duties or act as a trustee, which courts have not accepted. Multi-agent liability covers harm when several AI systems interact and no single human made the final decision. Deepfake evidence and the right to an explanation address how courts handle synthetic media and whether people can demand reasons for automated decisions.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is early and fragmented. No major jurisdiction has a settled rule for machine authorship, and the US Copyright Office has refused registration for works without human authorship, but litigation continues. Autonomous entities are not recognized as legal persons, so liability still attaches to developers, deployers, or users, though the lines are unclear. Multi-agent liability has almost no binding precedent, and courts are applying older doctrines like negligence and product liability case by case. Deepfake evidence rules are being tested, with some courts requiring authentication but no uniform standard. The right to an explanation exists in limited form under laws like GDPR for certain automated decisions, but it is narrow and rarely enforced. Across the cases tracked on this site, 142 are active lawsuits and 92 of them are intellectual property, which shows how much is still being argued rather than settled.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from creation to responsibility to evidence and explanation. The Threshold of Machine Authorship is the starting point for who owns AI output, and it connects to the intellectual property disputes counted in the active lawsuits. Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries examines whether an AI can hold a legal role, which matters before assigning blame. Liability When Agents Interact then takes up the harder problem of harm caused by multiple systems, where no single actor is obvious. Deepfakes and Evidentiary Standards shifts to the courtroom itself, asking how synthetic media can be admitted or challenged. The Right to an Explanation closes the section by looking at what a person can demand when an automated decision affects them.
